generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, this shows up in the small habits of a subject: the kinds of question that count as interesting, the sort of evidence that settles an argument, and the way disagreements are handled. Early on much of this is unspoken, picked up from how your lecturers reason and what your reading takes for granted rather than from anything set out plainly. Noticing those habits, and trying them in your own work, is how you start to take part rather than just look on.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students preparing for the same seminar on the same reading.

Student A reads the chapter once and highlights the key terms, ready to repeat the definitions if asked. The reading has been covered and the facts are in place. This is surface learning: the information has been taken in, but it sits on its own.

Student B reads the same chapter and keeps asking why. Why does the author reach this conclusion? How does it fit with last week's idea? Where might someone in the field disagree? By the seminar, Student B can connect the reading to a wider debate and take a position within it. This is deep learning: the ideas are linked into understanding that can be used and argued.

Both students have done the reading. Only Student B has taken the step your discourse community values, turning information into understanding.
generatedProse.summary: Learning at university means joining your subject's discourse community: a group that makes, tests and argues about knowledge together. You can now identify what makes that different from school, and begin to recognise the community of your own subject. The move from surface to deep learning, and the habits that support it, will matter in every lesson that follows.

check.body: Which of these would best help you recognise the discourse community of your own subject?

items.text: Noticing who produces and debates the key work in the field, and how they argue.
Counting how many facts your textbook contains.
Learning the timetable for your lectures.
Memorising the names of your tutors.

feedback.correct: That's right. You recognise a discourse community by seeing who makes its knowledge and how they argue, not by counting facts or learning logistics.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about how knowledge is made and argued, rather than facts or logistics.
feedback.incorrectFinal: You recognise your subject's discourse community by noticing who produces and debates its key work, and how they argue. The other options are about quantity or logistics, not how the community makes knowledge.

Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
